import Mathlib
/-! QED-M113: Big line or six visible points
Two points of a finite set in the plane see each other if the segment between them passes through no other point of the set. Prove that for every l there is an N such that any N points in the plane contain either l points on a line or 6 points that all see each other. This is known for 5 points that all see each other (for every l), and since 2026 for 6 such points when l = 4.
Informal statement: For finite $P\subset\mathbb R^2$, call $p,q\in P$ visible if $[p,q]\cap P=\{p,q\}$. Claim: for every $\ell\ge 3$ there is $N(\ell)$ such that every $P\subset\mathbb R^2$ with $|P|\ge N(\ell)$ contains $\ell$ collinear points or $6$ pairwise visible points.
Formalization notes:
* The plane is `ℝ × ℝ` (an affine space over itself); collinearity (`Collinear ℝ`) and closed
  segments (`segment ℝ p q`) are affine notions, so no Euclidean structure is needed.
* `Visible P p q` : every point of `P` on the closed segment `[p, q]` is an endpoint. For `p = q`
  this holds trivially; it only matters for distinct points of the 6-set `C`, which has 6 distinct
  elements because `C.card = 6`.
* "Contains `ℓ` collinear points": a subset `L ⊆ P` with `|L| = ℓ` that is collinear (equivalent to
  "at least `ℓ`", by taking subsets). "6 pairwise visible points": `C ⊆ P`, `|C| = 6`, all pairs
  visible with respect to the whole set `P` (not just `C`), as in the big-line-big-clique conjecture.
* `Claim` = the clique-6 row of the big-line-big-clique conjecture for every line size `ℓ ≥ 3`.
  `¬Claim` = some `ℓ` and arbitrarily large point sets with no `ℓ` collinear and no 6 mutually
  visible points. The hypothesis `3 ≤ ℓ` only excludes trivial cases (for `ℓ ≤ 2` any 2 points are
  collinear).
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDM113
noncomputable section

/-- `p` and `q` see each other in `P`: no point of `P` other than `p`, `q` lies on `[p, q]`. -/
def Visible (P : Finset (ℝ × ℝ)) (p q : ℝ × ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∀ r ∈ P, r ∈ segment ℝ p q → r = p ∨ r = q

/-- Every sufficiently large finite planar set has `ℓ` collinear points or 6 pairwise visible points. -/
def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ ℓ : ℕ, 3 ≤ ℓ → ∃ N : ℕ, ∀ P : Finset (ℝ × ℝ), N ≤ P.card →
    (∃ L : Finset (ℝ × ℝ), L ⊆ P ∧ L.card = ℓ ∧ Collinear ℝ (L : Set (ℝ × ℝ))) ∨
    (∃ C : Finset (ℝ × ℝ), C ⊆ P ∧ C.card = 6 ∧ ∀ p ∈ C, ∀ q ∈ C, Visible P p q)

end
end OpenProblems.QEDM113

title: Is there an aperiodic polyomino?
credit: Open problem as posed in A. Winslow, 'Some open problems in polyomino tilings' (DLT 2018); long-standing folklore (Golomb)
premise_risks: 'Polyomino' may be required to be simply connected in some sources; the Claim allows holes, which only makes the existence claim easier, so the vetter may prefer the simply connected version
existence proofs would likely be computer-assisted substitution arguments, heavy but finite in Lean
related to existing board items on hat/spectre tilings (M056, M057, N-117) but about a different tile class
plain: A polyomino is a shape made of unit squares glued edge to edge with no holes. In 2023 a single tile was found that tiles the plane only non-periodically, but it is built from kites, not squares. Is there a polyomino that tiles the plane (rotations and reflections allowed) but has no tiling that a translation maps onto itself?
math: A polyomino is a finite $P\subset\mathbb Z^2$ such that the union of the closed unit squares $c+[0,1]^2$, $c\in P$, is a closed topological disk. A tiling by $P$ is a set $\mathcal T$ of tiles $g(P)$, with $g(x)=Ax+b$, $A\in D_4\subset GL_2(\mathbb Z)$ and $b\in\mathbb Z^2$, that partition $\mathbb Z^2$. $P$ is aperiodic if some tiling exists but no tiling satisfies $\mathcal T+v=\mathcal T$ for any $v\in\mathbb Z^2\setminus\{0\}$. Problem: does an aperiodic polyomino exist? Board Claim: yes. A proof that every polyomino that tiles also has a periodic tiling settles the problem negatively. (Variant: allow holes, i.e. require only that $P$ is edge-connected.)
review_note: Known: Translations only: a polyomino tiles iff it tiles isohedrally/periodically (Wijshoff-van Leeuwen 1984; Beauquier-Nivat 1991). k-anisohedral polyominoes known for k<=6 (Winslow survey, Open Problem 6 asks for k>=7). Aperiodic sets of 3 polyominoes (with isometries) known; aperiodic sets of 2 polyominoes unknown (Winslow, Open Problem 8); translational aperiodic sets of 7 polyominoes (Yang-Zhang arXiv:2412.17382). Undecidability for sets of 5 polyominoes (Ollinger 2009). Non-polyomino aperiodic monotiles: hat and spectre (Smith-Myers-Kaplan-Goodman-Strauss 2023/24, Combinatorial Theory). Survey: A. Winslow, 'Some open problems in polyomino tilings', DLT 2018.
lean:
import Mathlib
/-! QED-M114: Is there an aperiodic polyomino?
A polyomino is a shape made of unit squares glued edge to edge with no holes. In 2023 a single tile was found that tiles the plane only non-periodically, but it is built from kites, not squares. Is there a polyomino that tiles the plane (rotations and reflections allowed) but has no tiling that a translation maps onto itself?
Informal statement: A polyomino is a finite $P\subset\mathbb Z^2$ such that the union of the closed unit squares $c+[0,1]^2$, $c\in P$, is a closed topological disk. A tiling by $P$ is a set $\mathcal T$ of tiles $g(P)$, with $g(x)=Ax+b$, $A\in D_4\subset GL_2(\mathbb Z)$ and $b\in\mathbb Z^2$, that partition $\mathbb Z^2$. $P$ is aperiodic if some tiling exists but no tiling satisfies $\mathcal T+v=\mathcal T$ for any $v\in\mathbb Z^2\setminus\{0\}$. Board Claim: an aperiodic polyomino exists.
Formalization notes:
* Cells are `ℤ × ℤ` (cell `c` is the closed square `c + [0,1]²`). Two cells are 4-adjacent
  (`Adj4`) if they share an edge (`|Δx| + |Δy| = 1`). `Conn4 S`: any two cells of `S` are joined by
  a path of 4-adjacent cells inside `S`.
* Polyomino (`IsPolyomino`): `P` finite (a `Finset`), nonempty, `P` 4-connected, and the complement
  `ℤ² \ P` 4-connected. This is the standard combinatorial characterization of "the union of the
  squares is a closed topological disk": if both are 4-connected then there are no holes (a bounded
  complement component would be a separate 4-component) and no pinch points (two diagonal cells of
  `P` whose other two neighbours at that corner are outside `P`: a 4-path in `P` joining the two
  diagonal cells closes up, with the diagonal, into an 8-connected closed curve of cells, which
  encloses one of the two outside corner cells and so cuts it off from the infinite complement,
  since 4-paths cannot cross 8-closed curves). Without holes or pinches the union is a compact
  connected 2-manifold with boundary in the plane with connected complement, hence a disk; the
  converse is immediate. (Using a homeomorphism to the closed disk directly would make
  any existence proof require a Schoenflies-type argument for the specific tile, so the
  combinatorial form is used.)
* `D₄` is enumerated as `Bool × Bool × Bool`: optionally swap coordinates, then optionally negate
  each coordinate. These are exactly the 8 signed permutation matrices, i.e. the full dihedral
  group `D₄ ⊂ GL₂(ℤ)` of the square lattice. Placed copy: `place P g b = {d4 g c + b | c ∈ P}`.
  (Applying `A` to cell labels rather than to squares just reindexes the cells of the image
  square set by a fixed lattice translation, which is absorbed into `b`.)
* A tiling is a SET of placed copies (sets of cells), not a family of placements, so a tile with
  symmetries is not counted twice; every cell lies in exactly one tile. Tiling `ℤ²` by cells is the
  same as tiling the plane by the closed unit squares (with interiors disjoint).
* Periodic: `T + v = T` for some `v ≠ 0` (translation of the set of tiles). `Aperiodic P`: some
  tiling exists and no tiling has any nonzero period (as in the informal statement). For a single
  tile in `ℤ²` (a 2D shift of finite type) this coincides with "no doubly periodic tiling", since
  a tiling with one period yields a doubly periodic one.
* `Claim` = an aperiodic polyomino exists. `¬Claim` = every polyomino that tiles the plane with
  rotations/reflections also admits a tiling with a nonzero translational period. Neither is
  vacuous: `IsTiling` is satisfiable (e.g. the monomino) and forces all tiles to be copies of `P`.
  The variant allowing holes (dropping the complement condition) is not encoded.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDM114
noncomputable section

/-- Edge adjacency of cells. -/
def Adj4 (a b : ℤ × ℤ) : Prop := |a.1 - b.1| + |a.2 - b.2| = 1

/-- `S` is 4-connected: any two of its cells are joined by an edge-adjacent path inside `S`. -/
def Conn4 (S : Set (ℤ × ℤ)) : Prop :=
  ∀ a ∈ S, ∀ b ∈ S,
    Relation.ReflTransGen (fun x y : ℤ × ℤ => x ∈ S ∧ y ∈ S ∧ Adj4 x y) a b

/-- Polyomino (simply connected): nonempty, 4-connected, with 4-connected complement. -/
def IsPolyomino (P : Finset (ℤ × ℤ)) : Prop :=
  P.Nonempty ∧ Conn4 (P : Set (ℤ × ℤ)) ∧ Conn4 ((P : Set (ℤ × ℤ))ᶜ)

/-- The 8 elements of `D₄ ⊂ GL₂(ℤ)`: optional coordinate swap, then optional sign changes. -/
def d4 (g : Bool × Bool × Bool) (c : ℤ × ℤ) : ℤ × ℤ :=
  let s : ℤ × ℤ := if g.1 then (c.2, c.1) else c
  ((if g.2.1 then -s.1 else s.1), (if g.2.2 then -s.2 else s.2))

/-- The copy `g(P) + b` of `P`. -/
def place (P : Finset (ℤ × ℤ)) (g : Bool × Bool × Bool) (b : ℤ × ℤ) : Set (ℤ × ℤ) :=
  {z : ℤ × ℤ | ∃ c ∈ P, z = d4 g c + b}

/-- `T` is a tiling of `ℤ²` by isometric copies of `P`. -/
def IsTiling (P : Finset (ℤ × ℤ)) (T : Set (Set (ℤ × ℤ))) : Prop :=
  (∀ t ∈ T, ∃ g : Bool × Bool × Bool, ∃ b : ℤ × ℤ, t = place P g b) ∧
    ∀ z : ℤ × ℤ, ∃! t : Set (ℤ × ℤ), t ∈ T ∧ z ∈ t

/-- Translate every tile of `T` by `v`. -/
def translateTiling (v : ℤ × ℤ) (T : Set (Set (ℤ × ℤ))) : Set (Set (ℤ × ℤ)) :=
  {t : Set (ℤ × ℤ) | ∃ s ∈ T, t = (fun z : ℤ × ℤ => z + v) '' s}

/-- `P` tiles, but no tiling by `P` has a nonzero translational period. -/
def Aperiodic (P : Finset (ℤ × ℤ)) : Prop :=
  (∃ T : Set (Set (ℤ × ℤ)), IsTiling P T) ∧
    ∀ T : Set (Set (ℤ × ℤ)), IsTiling P T → ∀ v : ℤ × ℤ, v ≠ 0 → translateTiling v T ≠ T

/-- There exists an aperiodic (simply connected) polyomino. -/
def Claim : Prop :=
  ∃ P : Finset (ℤ × ℤ), IsPolyomino P ∧ Aperiodic P

end
end OpenProblems.QEDM114

title: Returning to the identity in SL(3,Z)
credit: Open problem as recorded by I. Potapov and coauthors and in R. Dong's survey (2023)
premise_risks: Lean decidability statement via ComputablePred on lists of Fin 3 → Fin 3 → ℤ is easy to state; undecidability would need Turing-reduction infrastructure
plain: You are given finitely many 3x3 integer matrices with determinant 1. Can some nonempty product of them (in any order, with repetition) equal the identity matrix? For 2x2 matrices there is an algorithm, and for 4x4 matrices it is known that none exists. Decide whether an algorithm exists for 3x3.
math: Let $\mathcal I_3=\{(M_1,\dots,M_k): k\ge1,\ M_i\in SL(3,\mathbb Z),\ \exists\, m\ge1,\ i_1,\dots,i_m\in\{1,\dots,k\}:\ M_{i_1}\cdots M_{i_m}=I_3\}$, with instances given as finite lists of integer matrices. Problem: is $\mathcal I_3$ decidable? Board Claim: $\mathcal I_3$ is decidable. A proof of undecidability settles the problem negatively.
review_note: Known: SL(2,Z): identity and membership decidable (Choffrut-Karhumaki 2005; Bell-Potapov; Potapov-Semukhin for nonsingular 2x2 integer matrices, SODA 2017). 3x3: mortality (zero matrix) undecidable for Z^{3x3} (Paterson 1970), but the identity problem is not covered. SL(4,Z): identity problem undecidable (Bell-Potapov 2010, via F2 x F2). Identity problem decidable for the Heisenberg group H(3,Z) (Ko-Niskanen-Potapov, ICALP 2018, arXiv:1706.04166), for SA(2,Z) (Dong, arXiv:2301.09502), and for 4x4 unitriangular matrices (arXiv:2202.05225). Survey: R. Dong, 'Recent advances in algorithmic problems for semigroups', arXiv:2309.10943 (ACM SIGLOG News 2023): status of all listed problems open for SL(3,Z).

import Mathlib
/-! QED-M115: Returning to the identity in SL(3,Z)
You are given finitely many 3x3 integer matrices with determinant 1. Can some nonempty product of them (in any order, with repetition) equal the identity matrix? For 2x2 matrices there is an algorithm, and for 4x4 matrices it is known that none exists. Decide whether an algorithm exists for 3x3.
Informal statement: Let $\mathcal I_3=\{(M_1,\dots,M_k): k\ge1,\ M_i\in SL(3,\mathbb Z),\ \exists\, m\ge1,\ i_1,\dots,i_m\in\{1,\dots,k\}:\ M_{i_1}\cdots M_{i_m}=I_3\}$, with instances given as finite lists of integer matrices. Is $\mathcal I_3$ decidable? Board Claim: $\mathcal I_3$ is decidable.
Formalization notes:
* Instances are `List (Fin 3 → Fin 3 → ℕ)`: a list of 3×3 arrays of natural numbers, each entry
  decoded to an integer by the zig-zag bijection `zz : ℕ → ℤ` (`2n ↦ n`, `2n+1 ↦ -(n+1)`). This is a
  computable bijection, so it is just a `Primcodable` encoding of lists of integer matrices (it
  avoids relying on a `Primcodable ℤ` / `Matrix` instance). `toMat` turns an array into a
  `Matrix (Fin 3) (Fin 3) ℤ`.
* `Ident3 L`: every matrix in `L` has determinant 1 (membership in `SL(3,ℤ)`), and some NONEMPTY
  word `w` in the indices of `L` (repetition allowed, any order) has product `1`. The empty list
  is automatically a no-instance (`Fin 0` admits no nonempty word), matching `k ≥ 1`. Lists
  containing a matrix of determinant `≠ 1` are no-instances; since the determinant test is
  computable this does not change decidability (it is the language $\mathcal I_3$ literally).
* `List.prod` multiplies left to right, `M_{i_1} ⋯ M_{i_m}`; the order convention is irrelevant
  for the identity problem anyway (reverse words).
* Decidability is Mathlib's `ComputablePred`. `Claim` = the identity problem for `SL(3,ℤ)` is
  decidable; `¬Claim` = it is undecidable. The predicate is r.e. (enumerate words), so the content
  is co-r.e.-ness / an algorithm; neither side is trivial.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDM115
noncomputable section

/-- Zig-zag bijection `ℕ → ℤ`: `2n ↦ n`, `2n+1 ↦ -(n+1)`. -/
def zz (n : ℕ) : ℤ :=
  if n % 2 = 0 then ((n / 2 : ℕ) : ℤ) else -((n / 2 : ℕ) : ℤ) - 1

/-- The integer matrix encoded by a 3×3 array of codes. -/
def toMat (A : Fin 3 → Fin 3 → ℕ) : Matrix (Fin 3) (Fin 3) ℤ :=
  Matrix.of (fun i j : Fin 3 => zz (A i j))

/-- `L` is a list of `SL(3,ℤ)` matrices some nonempty product of which is the identity. -/
def Ident3 (L : List (Fin 3 → Fin 3 → ℕ)) : Prop :=
  (∀ A ∈ L, (toMat A).det = 1) ∧
    ∃ w : List (Fin L.length), w ≠ [] ∧
      (w.map (fun i : Fin L.length => toMat (L.get i))).prod = 1

/-- The identity problem for `SL(3,ℤ)` is decidable. -/
def Claim : Prop :=
  ComputablePred Ident3

end
end OpenProblems.QEDM115

title: Spectral gap of the spin-2 valence-bond-solid (AKLT) model on the square lattice
credit: Conjectured by Affleck, Kennedy, Lieb, Tasaki (1988); status per Pomata-Wei (2020) and Jackson-Nachtergaele-Young (2026).
premise_risks: Model named after people (AKLT), but the question is the spectral-gap property, not a named conjecture
Partly approachable by a large certified finite-size computation; could fall to a computer-assisted proof
Board already has AKLT on the hat (N-457) - related theme
plain: Put a quantum spin 2 (a 5-dimensional space) at every site of an L x L periodic square grid. For each edge, add the energy of projecting the two neighbouring spins onto their joint spin-4 state. The resulting Hamiltonian has ground energy 0, attained by the AKLT valence-bond state. Show that the first excited level stays a fixed distance above 0 however large L is. This gap was proved for the hexagonal lattice in 2020 and for many decorated square lattices, but not for the plain square lattice.
math: Let $\mathcal H_L=\bigotimes_{x\in(\mathbb Z/L\mathbb Z)^2}\mathbb C^5$, let $\mathbf S_x$ be the spin-2 operators at $x$, and for a nearest-neighbour edge $xy$ of the torus let $P^{(4)}_{xy}$ be the orthogonal projection onto the eigenspace $\{(\mathbf S_x+\mathbf S_y)^2=20\}$ (total spin 4). Let $H_L=\sum_{xy}P^{(4)}_{xy}$, so $H_L\ge0$ and $\ker H_L\neq\{0\}$. Prove there is $\gamma>0$ with $\mathrm{spec}(H_L)\subset\{0\}\cup[\gamma,\infty)$ for all $L\ge3$.

/-! QED-M116: Spectral gap of the spin-2 AKLT model on the square lattice

The resulting Hamiltonian has ground energy 0, attained by the AKLT valence-bond state. Show that the first excited level stays a fixed distance above 0 however large L is. This gap was proved for the hexagonal lattice in 2020 and for many decorated square lattices, but not for the plain square lattice.
Informal statement: Let $\mathcal H_L=\bigotimes_{x\in(\mathbb Z/L\mathbb Z)^2}\mathbb C^5$, let $\mathbf S_x$ be the
spin-2 operators at $x$, and for a nearest-neighbour edge $xy$ of the torus let $P^{(4)}_{xy}$ be the orthogonal

so $H_L\ge0$ and $\ker H_L\neq\{0\}$. Prove there is $\gamma>0$ with
$\mathrm{spec}(H_L)\subset\{0\}\cup[\gamma,\infty)$ for all $L\ge3$.
Formalization notes:
* Sites: the discrete torus `Fin L × Fin L` with periodic successor `succMod i = (i+1) mod L`.
  Each site `x` contributes the two edges `x — right x` and `x — up x`; for `L ≥ 3` these are
  the `2L²` nearest-neighbour edges of the torus, each counted exactly once, with no loops or
  multi-edges.
* Hilbert space: `ℂ^(Config L)` where `Config L = Site L → Fin 5` is the product basis
  (basis vector `k : Fin 5` at a site is the `S^z` eigenvector with `m = 2 - k`). Operators are
  matrices `Matrix (Config L) (Config L) ℂ`; this is exactly `⊗_x ℂ^5` in the product basis.
* Spin-2 matrices: `Sz = diag(2,1,0,-1,-2)`, `S⁺|m⟩ = √(6 - m(m+1)) |m+1⟩` (entries 2, √6, √6, 2
  on the superdiagonal), `S⁻ = (S⁺)ᵀ`. Two-site `S·S = Sz⊗Sz + ½(S⁺⊗S⁻ + S⁻⊗S⁺)`, and the
  two-site Casimir `C = (S₁+S₂)² = S₁² + S₂² + 2 S₁·S₂ = 12 + 2 S₁·S₂` (since `S² = s(s+1) = 6`).
  `C` is Hermitian with spectrum `{j(j+1) : j = 0..4} = {0,2,6,12,20}`, so the spectral
  projection onto `C = 20` (total spin 4, a 9-dimensional space) is the Lagrange polynomial
  `P4 = C(C-2)(C-6)(C-12)/(20·18·14·8)`, `20·18·14·8 = 40320`. (Checked numerically: `P4² = P4`,
  `tr P4 = 9`.)
* Embedding at an edge `(x,y)`: matrix entry `⟨σ|P_{xy}|τ⟩ = P4[(σx,σy),(τx,τy)]` if `σ` and `τ`
  agree off `{x,y}`, else 0. The off-edge agreement is written decidably as
  `τ = update (update σ x (τ x)) y (τ y)`.
* Gap: `H L` is Hermitian and positive semidefinite, so its spectrum is real and ⊆ [0,∞);
  the spectrum of a finite matrix is its set of eigenvalues, stated here directly via
  `H.mulVec v = μ • v`, `v ≠ 0`. `Claim`: one `γ > 0` works for all `L ≥ 3` — no eigenvalue in
  `(0, γ)` (kernel degeneracy allowed). Each fixed `L` trivially has some positive gap, so `Claim`
  is equivalent to `inf_{L ≥ 3} gap(H_L) > 0`, the uniform spectral gap of the AKLT literature.
  Proving `¬Claim` = the gaps above the ground space tend to 0 along a sequence of `L`
  (gaplessness).
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDM116
noncomputable section

/-- Sites of the `L × L` discrete torus. -/
abbrev Site (L : ℕ) : Type := Fin L × Fin L

/-- Product-basis labels: a spin-2 basis state (`k : Fin 5`, `m = 2 - k`) at each site. -/
abbrev Config (L : ℕ) : Type := Site L → Fin 5

/-- Periodic successor `i ↦ (i + 1) mod L`. -/
def succMod {L : ℕ} (i : Fin L) : Fin L :=
  ⟨(i.val + 1) % L, Nat.mod_lt _ (Nat.lt_of_le_of_lt (Nat.zero_le _) i.isLt)⟩

/-- Horizontal neighbour. -/
def right {L : ℕ} (x : Site L) : Site L := (succMod x.1, x.2)

/-- Vertical neighbour. -/
def up {L : ℕ} (x : Site L) : Site L := (x.1, succMod x.2)

/-- Spin-2 `S^z = diag(2,1,0,-1,-2)`. -/
def Sz : Matrix (Fin 5) (Fin 5) ℂ := Matrix.diagonal ![2, 1, 0, -1, -2]

/-- Spin-2 raising operator, `S⁺|m⟩ = √(6 - m(m+1)) |m+1⟩`. -/
def Splus : Matrix (Fin 5) (Fin 5) ℂ :=
  Matrix.of ![![0, 2, 0, 0, 0],
              ![0, 0, (Real.sqrt 6 : ℂ), 0, 0],
              ![0, 0, 0, (Real.sqrt 6 : ℂ), 0],
              ![0, 0, 0, 0, 2],
              ![0, 0, 0, 0, 0]]

/-- Spin-2 lowering operator `S⁻ = (S⁺)ᵀ` (real entries). -/
def Sminus : Matrix (Fin 5) (Fin 5) ℂ := Splus.transpose

/-- Kronecker product of two single-site operators. -/
def kron2 (A B : Matrix (Fin 5) (Fin 5) ℂ) : Matrix (Fin 5 × Fin 5) (Fin 5 × Fin 5) ℂ :=
  Matrix.of fun p q => A p.1 q.1 * B p.2 q.2

/-- `S₁·S₂ = Sz⊗Sz + ½ (S⁺⊗S⁻ + S⁻⊗S⁺)`. -/
def SdotS : Matrix (Fin 5 × Fin 5) (Fin 5 × Fin 5) ℂ :=
  kron2 Sz Sz + (1 / 2 : ℂ) • (kron2 Splus Sminus + kron2 Sminus Splus)

/-- Two-site Casimir `(S₁ + S₂)² = 12 + 2 S₁·S₂`, spectrum `{0, 2, 6, 12, 20}`. -/
def casimir : Matrix (Fin 5 × Fin 5) (Fin 5 × Fin 5) ℂ :=
  (12 : ℂ) • (1 : Matrix (Fin 5 × Fin 5) (Fin 5 × Fin 5) ℂ) + (2 : ℂ) • SdotS

/-- Orthogonal projection onto total spin 4 (`casimir = 20`). -/
def P4 : Matrix (Fin 5 × Fin 5) (Fin 5 × Fin 5) ℂ :=
  (1 / 40320 : ℂ) •
    (casimir * (casimir - (2 : ℂ) • (1 : Matrix (Fin 5 × Fin 5) (Fin 5 × Fin 5) ℂ)) *
      (casimir - (6 : ℂ) • (1 : Matrix (Fin 5 × Fin 5) (Fin 5 × Fin 5) ℂ)) *
      (casimir - (12 : ℂ) • (1 : Matrix (Fin 5 × Fin 5) (Fin 5 × Fin 5) ℂ)))

/-- `P4` acting on the sites `x, y` of the torus (identity elsewhere). -/
def edgeOp {L : ℕ} (x y : Site L) : Matrix (Config L) (Config L) ℂ :=
  Matrix.of fun σ τ : Config L =>
    if τ = Function.update (Function.update σ x (τ x)) y (τ y) then
      P4 (σ x, σ y) (τ x, τ y)
    else 0

/-- The spin-2 AKLT Hamiltonian on the `L × L` torus: one `P4` per nearest-neighbour edge. -/
def H (L : ℕ) : Matrix (Config L) (Config L) ℂ :=
  ∑ x : Site L, (edgeOp x (right x) + edgeOp x (up x))

/-- Uniform spectral gap: some `γ > 0` such that, for every `L ≥ 3`, every eigenvalue of `H L`
is `0` or has real part at least `γ` (all eigenvalues are real since `H L` is Hermitian). -/
def Claim : Prop :=
  ∃ γ : ℝ, 0 < γ ∧ ∀ L : ℕ, 3 ≤ L →
    ∀ (μ : ℂ) (v : Config L → ℂ), v ≠ 0 → (H L).mulVec v = μ • v → μ = 0 ∨ γ ≤ μ.re

end
end OpenProblems.QEDM116

title: An exponential improvement of the diagonal Ramsey lower bound
credit: Erdős (1947 bound and question); Spencer (1975)
premise_risks: Extremely famous and hard: low novelty, may be judged a famous problem stated directly
Not a person-named conjecture (Erdős offered a prize for the limit of R(k)^{1/k}, a stronger question)
Context only: refereed status of Ma–Shen–Xie (arXiv 2025, covered by Quanta 2026) not verified; 2605.25843 is an unrefereed 2026 preprint
plain: The Ramsey number R(k) is the least N such that every red/blue colouring of the edges of the complete graph K_N contains a one-coloured K_k. Erdos's 1947 random-colouring argument gives R(k) > (sqrt 2)^k, and in nearly 80 years only the constant factor in front has improved. Is there a fixed eps > 0 with R(k) > (sqrt 2 + eps)^k for all large k?
math: Prove that there exists $\varepsilon>0$ such that $R(k,k)\ge(\sqrt2+\varepsilon)^k$ for all sufficiently large $k$; equivalently, for every large $k$ there is a graph on $N\ge(\sqrt2+\varepsilon)^k$ vertices with no clique and no independent set of size $k$. (Best known: $R(k,k)\ge(1+o(1))\frac{\sqrt2}{e}\,k\,2^{k/2}$, Spencer 1975.)

/-! QED-M117: An exponential improvement of the diagonal Ramsey lower bound

Erdos's 1947 random-colouring argument gives R(k) > (sqrt 2)^k, and in nearly 80 years only the constant factor in front has improved. Is there a fixed eps > 0 with R(k) > (sqrt 2 + eps)^k for all large k?

* We use the graph form: a red/blue colouring of `K_N` is a simple graph `G` on `Fin N`
  (red = edge of `G`); a monochromatic `K_k` is a `k`-clique of `G` or of its complement `Gᶜ`.
  Mathlib's `SimpleGraph.CliqueFree k` says there is no `k`-clique, so a graph on `Fin N` with
  `G.CliqueFree k ∧ Gᶜ.CliqueFree k` witnesses `R(k,k) > N`.
* `Claim`: there is `ε > 0` such that for all sufficiently large `k` such a graph exists on
  `N ≥ (√2 + ε)^k` vertices. This gives `R(k,k) > (√2+ε)^k`; conversely `R(k,k) ≥ (√2+ε)^k`
  for all large `k` gives `Claim` with `ε/2` in place of `ε` (take `N = R(k,k) - 1`), so the
  two forms are equivalent. `¬Claim` means: for every `ε > 0`, `R(k,k) < (√2+ε)^k + 1` for

-/

title: Exponentially beat the 2^{-n} sphere-packing lower bound
credit: Minkowski; Klartag; Kabatiansky–Levenshtein
plain: In high dimension n the best sphere packings known have density only about n²·2^{-n} (up to log factors), barely above the trivial 2^{-n} from greedy/saturated packings, while the best upper bound is about 2^{-0.599n}. Is there a constant c>1 with packings of density at least c^n·2^{-n} in all large dimensions?
math: Let $\Delta_n$ be the supremum of upper densities of packings of congruent balls in $\mathbb{R}^n$. Prove or disprove: there exist $c>1$ and $N$ such that $\Delta_n\ge c^n2^{-n}$ for all $n\ge N$.

import Mathlib
/-! QED-M118: Exponentially beat Minkowski's sphere packing lower bound
In high dimension n the best sphere packings known have density only about n²·2^{-n} (up to log
factors), barely above the trivial 2^{-n} from greedy/saturated packings, while the best upper bound
is about 2^{-0.599n}. Is there a constant c>1 with packings of density at least c^n·2^{-n} in all
large dimensions?
Informal statement: Let $\Delta_n$ be the supremum of upper densities of packings of congruent balls
in $\mathbb{R}^n$. Prove or disprove: there exist $c>1$ and $N$ such that $\Delta_n\ge c^n2^{-n}$ for
all $n\ge N$.
Formalization notes:
* Space: `EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n)` with its `volume` (Lebesgue measure) and Euclidean metric.
  The definitions follow the packing-density definitions of QED-E040, specialised to balls.
* Packing: congruent copies of the closed unit ball are exactly its translates (the ball is
  invariant under orthogonal maps), so a packing is a sequence of centres `x : ℕ → E` with
  `dist (x i) (x j) ≥ 2` for `i ≠ j`, i.e. the balls have pairwise disjoint interiors (they may
  touch). Indexing by ℕ loses nothing: a ball packing is countable, and finite packings have
  density 0. The radius 1 is no loss since density is scale-invariant.
* Density: upper density = limsup over R → ∞ of vol(⋃ balls ∩ B(0,R)) / vol(B(0,R)), computed in
  `ℝ≥0∞` (numerator ≤ denominator < ∞, denominator > 0 for R > 0 and n ≥ 1). Δ_n is the supremum
  over packings (the standard definition, as in Rogers / Conway–Sloane; limsup vs lim and centring
  at the origin do not change the supremum).
* `Claim` = ∃ c > 1, ∃ N, ∀ n ≥ N, Δ_n ≥ (c/2)^n. Since Δ_n is a supremum, this is equivalent (after
  shrinking c) to the existence of individual packings of density ≥ c^n 2^{-n}. Proving `¬Claim` =
  for every c > 1 there are infinitely many n with Δ_n < c^n 2^{-n}, i.e. no exponential improvement
  over 2^{-n} holds in all large dimensions.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDM118
noncomputable section
open scoped ENNReal

/-- Ambient Euclidean space `ℝⁿ`. -/
abbrev E (n : ℕ) : Type := EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n)

/-- A packing of unit balls with centres `x i`: distinct centres are at distance at least 2. -/
def IsPacking {n : ℕ} (x : ℕ → E n) : Prop :=
  ∀ i j : ℕ, i ≠ j → 2 ≤ dist (x i) (x j)

/-- Fraction of the ball of radius `R` about the origin covered by the packing. -/
def coveredFraction {n : ℕ} (x : ℕ → E n) (R : ℝ) : ℝ≥0∞ :=
  MeasureTheory.volume ((⋃ i : ℕ, Metric.closedBall (x i) 1) ∩ Metric.ball (0 : E n) R) /
    MeasureTheory.volume (Metric.ball (0 : E n) R)

/-- Upper density of a packing: `limsup_{R → ∞}` of the covered fraction. -/
def upperDensity {n : ℕ} (x : ℕ → E n) : ℝ≥0∞ :=
  Filter.limsup (fun R : ℝ => coveredFraction x R) Filter.atTop

/-- Sphere packing density `Δ_n` of `ℝⁿ`. -/
def packingDensity (n : ℕ) : ℝ≥0∞ :=
  ⨆ (x : ℕ → E n) (_ : IsPacking x), upperDensity x

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∃ c : ℝ, 1 < c ∧ ∃ N : ℕ, ∀ n : ℕ, N ≤ n → ENNReal.ofReal ((c / 2) ^ n) ≤ packingDensity n

end
end OpenProblems.QEDM118

title: The 3k−4 conjecture modulo a prime
credit: Problem line from Freiman's 3k−4 theorem over Z. The mod-p conjecture appears in work of Freiman, Rödseth, Serra–Zémor, Candela–Serra–Spiegel, Lev–Serra and Grynkiewicz.
premise_risks: The name contains 'Freiman' only through 'Freiman's 3k−4 theorem' over Z. The mod-p statement is usually called 'the 3k−4 conjecture', which is not person-named.
A sparse-range improvement beyond 2.7652 may exist in a 2024–26 preprint not surfaced by search.
plain: Over the integers, Freiman's 3k−4 theorem says that if a finite set A has a sumset A+A with at most 3|A|−4 elements, then A lies in an arithmetic progression with only |A+A|−|A|+1 terms. Modulo a prime p the same should hold as long as A+A does not come too close to filling Z/pZ. It is known for tiny sets (|A| below roughly p/10^215) and, for larger sets, only when |A+A| is well below 3|A|. Prove the full statement.
math: Let $p$ be prime and $A\subseteq\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z$ with $A+A\neq\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z$. Write $|A+A|=2|A|+r$. Prove that if $|A+A|\le\min\{3|A|-4,\;p-r-4\}$, then $A$ is contained in an arithmetic progression $\{a,a+d,\dots,a+(L-1)d\}$ with $L\le |A|+r+1=|A+A|-|A|+1$. (This states only the first conclusion of the full conjecture, arXiv:1909.07967 Conj. 1.2; the companion statement that $2A$ contains an arithmetic progression with the same difference and at least $2|A|-1$ terms is omitted.)

Modulo a prime p the same should hold as long as A+A does not come too close to filling Z/pZ. title: Superlinear exponent for K_t-intersecting graph families
credit: Full conjecture by Ellis, Filmus, Friedgut (generalising the Simonovits–Sós triangle question). Superlinear-exponent formulation by the proposer. Bounds by Berger–Zhao, Mani–Zhang, Sason.
premise_risks: The full statement is often called the 'Ellis–Filmus–Friedgut conjecture'. This candidate is an unnamed weaker sub-question, which the naming rule allows.
The t=5 result is a 2025 PRIMES report, possibly unrefereed. It is used only for context.
A cleverer entropy or recursive-trace argument might give a superlinear exponent fairly easily. I could not find one, but this is a difficulty risk.
plain: Consider a family of graphs on the same n labelled vertices such that any two graphs in the family share a complete subgraph K_t among their common edges. Taking all graphs that contain one fixed K_t gives a fraction 2^{-t(t-1)/2} of all graphs, and this is believed to be optimal. An easy entropy argument shows the best possible fraction is at most about 2^{-2t}, so the exponent is at least linear in t. Prove that the exponent grows faster than linearly: the largest fraction is at most 2^{-f(t)} with f(t)/t tending to infinity.
math: Call $\mathcal F\subseteq 2^{E(K_n)}$ $K_t$-intersecting if for all $G,H\in\mathcal F$ the graph $G\cap H$ contains a copy of $K_t$. Let $\alpha_t=\sup_n\max\{|\mathcal F|\,2^{-\binom n2}:\mathcal F\text{ is }K_t\text{-intersecting on }[n]\}$ and $f(t)=\log_2(1/\alpha_t)$. Prove $f(t)/t\to\infty$. (Known: $f(t)\le\binom t2$; $f(3)=3,f(4)=6,f(5)=10$; Shearer's lemma over a uniformly random partition of $[n]$ into $m$ parts gives $f(t)\ge m\,f(\lceil t/m\rceil)$, hence $f(t)\ge 10\lfloor t/5\rfloor$ and $\lim f(t)/t=\sup_s f(s)/s$. So the claim is equivalent to: for every $C$ there is $s$ with $\alpha_s\le 2^{-Cs}$. Conjectured: $f(t)=\binom t2$.)

Formalization notes:
* Labelled graphs on [n] = Fin n are encoded as edge sets G ⊆ `pairs n`, where `pairs n` is the set of ordered pairs
  (i, j) with i < j (one representative per unordered pair; |pairs n| = C(n,2)). So graphs on [n] correspond
  bijectively to subsets of `pairs n`, and there are 2^{C(n,2)} of them.
* `KtIntersecting t F`: for all G, H ∈ F (G = H allowed, as in the definition), there is a t-element vertex set s all
  of whose pairs i < j in s are edges of both G and H, i.e. G ∩ H contains a copy of K_t (s.card = t forces t
  distinct vertices).
* `frac n t` = (max |F| over K_t-intersecting families of graphs on [n]) / 2^{C(n,2)} ∈ [0, 1]. `alpha t` = sup over n
  (a real `iSup` of a sequence bounded by 1, hence a genuine supremum). alpha t > 0, witnessed by n = t and
  F = {complete graph}, so f(t) = log₂(1/alpha t) is a genuine real number.
* `Claim`: f(t)/t → ∞ as t → ∞ (t cast to ℝ). Proving ¬Claim = f(t)/t is bounded along a subsequence (by the
  known super-additivity, f(t)/t then converges to a finite limit).
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDM120
noncomputable section
open scoped Classical

/-- Potential edges of a graph on Fin n, as pairs (i, j) with i < j. -/
def pairs (n : ℕ) : Finset (Fin n × Fin n) :=
  (Finset.univ : Finset (Fin n × Fin n)).filter (fun p : Fin n × Fin n => p.1 < p.2)

/-- Every two members (not necessarily distinct) share a copy of K_t in their common edges. -/
def KtIntersecting {n : ℕ} (t : ℕ) (F : Finset (Finset (Fin n × Fin n))) : Prop :=
  ∀ G ∈ F, ∀ H ∈ F, ∃ s : Finset (Fin n), s.card = t ∧
    ∀ i ∈ s, ∀ j ∈ s, i < j → (i, j) ∈ G ∧ (i, j) ∈ H

/-- A family of graphs on Fin n: all members are edge sets inside `pairs n`. -/
def IsGraphFamily {n : ℕ} (F : Finset (Finset (Fin n × Fin n))) : Prop :=
  ∀ G ∈ F, G ⊆ pairs n

/-- Largest fraction of all labelled graphs on [n] forming a K_t-intersecting family. -/
def frac (n t : ℕ) : ℝ :=
  ((((Finset.univ : Finset (Finset (Finset (Fin n × Fin n)))).filter
      (fun F : Finset (Finset (Fin n × Fin n)) => IsGraphFamily F ∧ KtIntersecting t F)).sup
      Finset.card : ℕ) : ℝ) / (2 : ℝ) ^ (Nat.choose n 2)

/-- α_t = sup_n frac n t. -/
def alpha (t : ℕ) : ℝ := ⨆ n : ℕ, frac n t

/-- f(t) = log₂(1/α_t). -/
def f (t : ℕ) : ℝ := Real.logb 2 (1 / alpha t)

def Claim : Prop :=
  Filter.Tendsto (fun t : ℕ => f t / (t : ℝ)) Filter.atTop Filter.atTop

end
end OpenProblems.QEDM120

plain: Take several bases of the vector space (Z/p)^n and pool all their vectors into one list. /-! QED-M121: Additive basis conjecture: a constant number of bases suffices
Take several bases of the vector space (Z/p)^n and pool all their vectors into one list. Can every vector of the space be written as the sum of some sub-list, using each pooled vector at most once? The conjecture says a fixed number c(p) of bases always suffices, independent of the dimension n. The best proven bound grows like log n.
Informal statement: For a prime $p$, a finite multiset $B$ of vectors in $\mathbb{F}_p^n$ is an additive basis if $\{\sum_{b\in B}\varepsilon_b b : \varepsilon\in\{0,1\}^B\}=\mathbb{F}_p^n$. Prove that for every prime $p$ there is $c(p)$ such that for every $n\ge1$ and all bases $B_1,\dots,B_{c(p)}$ of $\mathbb{F}_p^n$, the multiset union $B_1\uplus\cdots\uplus B_{c(p)}$ is an additive basis.

* 𝔽_p^n is `Fin n → ZMod p`. A basis is an indexed family `B a : Fin n → (Fin n → ZMod p)` that
  is linearly independent over `ZMod p`; since the space has dimension n, n linearly independent
  vectors are exactly a basis (we avoid the `Basis` structure, whose namespace has moved).
* The multiset union of c bases is the family indexed by `Fin c × Fin n`; repeated vectors across
  bases are separate members, as in a multiset. A 0/1 choice is `ε : Fin c → Fin n → Bool`, and
  the subset sum is `∑ a, ∑ i, if ε a i then B a i else 0`.

  every target vector v, some subset sum equals v. n ≥ 1 rules out the trivial n = 0 case (it
  is harmless anyway); c = 0 never works for n ≥ 1, so the existential is not vacuous.
  ¬Claim: for some prime p, for every c there is a dimension and c bases whose union is not an
  additive basis.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDM121

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ p : ℕ, p.Prime → ∃ c : ℕ, ∀ n : ℕ, 1 ≤ n →
    ∀ B : Fin c → Fin n → (Fin n → ZMod p),
      (∀ a : Fin c, LinearIndependent (ZMod p) (B a)) →
      ∀ v : Fin n → ZMod p, ∃ ε : Fin c → Fin n → Bool,
        v = ∑ a : Fin c, ∑ i : Fin n, (if ε a i then B a i else 0)

end OpenProblems.QEDM121

title: The widest hollow body in 3-space

plain: A convex body is hollow if no point with all-integer coordinates lies strictly inside it. Hollow bodies must be thin in some integer direction (the flatness theorem). /-! QED-M123: Halving planes in 3-space: beat n^{5/2}
Take n points in 3-space, with n odd and no four on a common plane. A halving triangle is a triple of the points whose plane splits the remaining n-3 points evenly, half on each side. The best upper bound on the number of halving triangles, about n^{5/2}, has not been improved since 2001. Show that the exponent 5/2 can be lowered.
Informal statement: For $S\subset\mathbb{R}^3$ with $|S|=n$ odd and no four points coplanar, let $h(S)$ be the number of $3$-subsets $T\subseteq S$ such that each open half-space bounded by $\operatorname{aff}(T)$ contains exactly $(n-3)/2$ points of $S$. Prove that there exist $\varepsilon>0$ and $C$ with $h(S)\le C\,n^{5/2-\varepsilon}$ for all such $S$.
Formalization notes:
* E = `EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 3)`. "No four coplanar": every 4-subset T has vector span of
  dimension 3 (`Module.finrank ℝ (vectorSpan ℝ T) = 3`), i.e. is affinely spanning.
  Consequently every 3-subset is affinely independent and spans a unique plane, and no
  fourth point of S lies on it.
* A plane is {x | ⟪a,x⟫ = b} with a ≠ 0. T is halving if some such plane contains T and
  has exactly (n−3)/2 points of S strictly on each side. Since aff(T) is the unique plane
  through T, this is exactly the informal definition. (n−3)/2 is natural division; n is odd
  and n ≥ 3 whenever a 3-subset exists, so it is exact.
* The bound is C·n^{5/2−ε} with real exponent (`Real.rpow`); C and ε are uniform in S.
  For n = 1 the count is 0, so small cases impose no extra constraint.
* `Claim` is the power-saving improvement of Sharir–Smorodinsky–Tardos. `¬Claim` says for every
  ε > 0 the exponent 5/2 − ε fails (the O(n^{5/2}) bound is tight up to n^{o(1)}).
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDM123
noncomputable section
open scoped InnerProductSpace RealInnerProductSpace

abbrev E := EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 3)

/-- No four points of `S` are coplanar. -/
def NoFourCoplanar (S : Finset E) : Prop :=
  ∀ T : Finset E, T ⊆ S → T.card = 4 → Module.finrank ℝ (vectorSpan ℝ (T : Set E)) = 3

/-- `T` is a halving triangle of `S`. -/
def IsHalving (S T : Finset E) : Prop :=
  ∃ (a : E) (b : ℝ), a ≠ 0 ∧ (∀ x ∈ T, ⟪a, x⟫_ℝ = b) ∧
    (S.filter (fun x : E => b < ⟪a, x⟫_ℝ)).card = (S.card - 3) / 2 ∧
    (S.filter (fun x : E => ⟪a, x⟫_ℝ < b)).card = (S.card - 3) / 2

open Classical in
/-- Number of halving triangles. -/
def h (S : Finset E) : ℕ :=
  ((S.powersetCard 3).filter (fun T : Finset E => IsHalving S T)).card

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∃ ε : ℝ, 0 < ε ∧ ∃ C : ℝ, ∀ S : Finset E, Odd S.card → NoFourCoplanar S →
    (h S : ℝ) ≤ C * (S.card : ℝ) ^ ((5 : ℝ) / 2 - ε)

end
end OpenProblems.QEDM123

/-! QED-M124: The 1/3–2/3 conjecture for width-three posets
Take a finite partial order and pick one of its linear extensions (total orders compatible with it) uniformly at random. The 1/3–2/3 conjecture says that, unless the order is already total, some pair x, y has probability between 1/3 and 2/3 that x comes before y. It is known for width 2 (no three pairwise incomparable elements) and, since 2026, for all posets of width above some unspecified constant. Prove it for every poset of width 3.
Informal statement: For a finite poset $P$, let $e(P)$ be its number of linear extensions and, for $x\ne y$, let $p(x\prec y)$ be the fraction of linear extensions in which $x$ precedes $y$. Prove that every finite poset of width exactly $3$ contains $x,y$ with $\tfrac13\le p(x\prec y)\le\tfrac23$.
Formalization notes:
* A finite poset is a type `α : Type` with `[Fintype α] [PartialOrder α]` (every finite poset is
  isomorphic to one, and the statement is isomorphism invariant).
* A linear extension is a bijection `f : α ≃ Fin (Fintype.card α)` that is strictly order
  preserving: `x < y → f x < f y`. These correspond bijectively to linear extensions.
* `numLinExt α` = number of linear extensions; `numBefore x y` = number in which `f x < f y`.
  Both are `Nat.card` of finite subtypes (finite since `α ≃ Fin _` is finite), so no junk value.
* Width exactly 3: some 3-element antichain exists, and every antichain (as a Finset) has at most
  3 elements. Antichains use `IsAntichain (· ≤ ·)`.
* Claim: every such poset has x ≠ y with 1/3 ≤ numBefore x y / numLinExt ≤ 2/3, written without
  division as 3·numBefore ≥ numLinExt and 3·numBefore ≤ 2·numLinExt (numLinExt ≥ 1 since
  linear extensions exist). ¬Claim: some width-3 poset has no balanced pair.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDM124
noncomputable section

/-- Number of linear extensions of a finite poset. -/
def numLinExt (α : Type) [Fintype α] [PartialOrder α] : ℕ :=
  Nat.card {f : α ≃ Fin (Fintype.card α) // ∀ x y : α, x < y → f x < f y}

/-- Number of linear extensions in which `x` comes before `y`. -/
def numBefore {α : Type} [Fintype α] [PartialOrder α] (x y : α) : ℕ :=
  Nat.card {f : α ≃ Fin (Fintype.card α) // (∀ a b : α, a < b → f a < f b) ∧ f x < f y}

/-- The poset has width exactly 3. -/
def WidthThree (α : Type) [Fintype α] [PartialOrder α] : Prop :=
  (∃ s : Finset α, s.card = 3 ∧ IsAntichain (· ≤ ·) (s : Set α)) ∧
    ∀ s : Finset α, IsAntichain (· ≤ ·) (s : Set α) → s.card ≤ 3

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ (α : Type) [Fintype α] [PartialOrder α], WidthThree α →
    ∃ x y : α, x ≠ y ∧ numLinExt α ≤ 3 * numBefore x y ∧ 3 * numBefore x y ≤ 2 * numLinExt α

end
end OpenProblems.QEDM124

A matroid of rank r is sparse paving if its non-bases are r-sets, no two of which share r−1 elements; equivalently, all circuits have size r or r+1, and so do all circuits of its dual. These are the 'generic' matroids, and it is believed that almost all matroids on n labelled elements are of this kind. Even the much weaker statement is open: show that a fixed positive fraction of all matroids on n elements are sparse paving, for all large n.
Informal statement: Let $m_n$ be the number of matroids on the ground set $[n]$ and $s_n$ the number of sparse paving matroids on $[n]$ (rank $r$ matroids whose set $\mathcal N$ of non-bases is a family of $r$-subsets with $|X\triangle Y|\ge 4$ for distinct $X,Y\in\mathcal N$). Claim: $\liminf_{n\to\infty} s_n/m_n>0$.
Formalization notes:
* A matroid on the labelled ground set `Fin n` is identified with its family of bases
  ℬ ⊆ 2^[n], characterised by the standard base axioms: ℬ nonempty, and the exchange axiom
  (for B₁, B₂ ∈ ℬ and x ∈ B₁ \ B₂ there is y ∈ B₂ \ B₁ with (B₁ − x) + y ∈ ℬ). This is a
  bijection between matroids on [n] and such families, so `m n` counts labelled matroids.
  (All bases then have a common size, the rank.)
* Sparse paving: there is r such that every base has size r, and the non-bases
  𝒩 = (r-subsets) \ ℬ satisfy |X Δ Y| ≥ 4 for distinct X, Y ∈ 𝒩, with X Δ Y written as
  (X \ Y) ∪ (Y \ X). `s n` counts base families that are both matroids and sparse paving.
* m n ≥ 1 (e.g. ℬ = {∅}), so liminf s_n/m_n > 0 is equivalent to: ∃ c > 0 and N₀ with
  c·m n ≤ s n for all n ≥ N₀. That is `Claim`. `¬Claim` means liminf s_n/m_n = 0.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDM125
noncomputable section
open Classical

/-- `ℬ` satisfies the matroid base axioms on ground set `Fin n`. -/
def IsMatroidBases {n : ℕ} (ℬ : Finset (Finset (Fin n))) : Prop :=
  ℬ.Nonempty ∧
    ∀ B₁ ∈ ℬ, ∀ B₂ ∈ ℬ, ∀ x ∈ B₁ \ B₂, ∃ y ∈ B₂ \ B₁, insert y (B₁.erase x) ∈ ℬ

/-- The matroid with bases `ℬ` is sparse paving. -/
def IsSparsePaving {n : ℕ} (ℬ : Finset (Finset (Fin n))) : Prop :=
  ∃ r : ℕ, (∀ B ∈ ℬ, B.card = r) ∧
    ∀ X ∈ (Finset.univ : Finset (Fin n)).powersetCard r \ ℬ,
    ∀ Y ∈ (Finset.univ : Finset (Fin n)).powersetCard r \ ℬ,
      X ≠ Y → 4 ≤ ((X \ Y) ∪ (Y \ X)).card

/-- Number of matroids on `Fin n`. -/
def m (n : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  ((Finset.univ : Finset (Finset (Finset (Fin n)))).filter
    (fun ℬ : Finset (Finset (Fin n)) => IsMatroidBases ℬ)).card

/-- Number of sparse paving matroids on `Fin n`. -/
def s (n : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  ((Finset.univ : Finset (Finset (Finset (Fin n)))).filter
    (fun ℬ : Finset (Finset (Fin n)) => IsMatroidBases ℬ ∧ IsSparsePaving ℬ)).card

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∃ c : ℝ, 0 < c ∧ ∃ N₀ : ℕ, ∀ n : ℕ, N₀ ≤ n → c * (m n : ℝ) ≤ (s n : ℝ)

end
end OpenProblems.QEDM125

title: Glauber dynamics for colourings mixes rapidly with (1+eps)Delta colours
credit: Conjecture q >= Delta+2 commonly cited to Jerrum (1995) as a 'long-standing conjecture'; asymptotic form as stated here is a weaker unnamed version.
premise_risks: Actively moving constant (Tao-list-style risk): new 2026 preprints (Li-Oveis Gharan, Yang) unrefereed; the endpoint target avoids arbitrary intermediate thresholds
Some sources call the Delta+2 statement 'Jerrum's conjecture'; the asymptotic version is the unnamed weaker form
Well known, so low novelty
plain: To sample a random proper colouring of a graph with q colours, repeat this step: pick a random vertex and a random colour, and recolour the vertex if no neighbour already has that colour. For large maximum degree Delta this chain is known to reach equilibrium in polynomial time once q is a bit above (1+1/e)Delta, about 1.368 Delta (2026). Conjecturally q >= Delta+2 is enough. Weakest asymptotic form: for every eps > 0, are (1+eps)Delta colours enough once Delta is large?
math: For a finite graph $G$ on $n$ vertices with maximum degree $\Delta$ and an integer $q\ge\Delta+2$, let $\Omega$ be the set of proper $q$-colourings and $P$ the Glauber (Metropolis) chain on $\Omega$: choose $v\in V$ and $c\in[q]$ uniformly at random and set $\sigma(v)=c$ if no neighbour of $v$ has colour $c$. Let $t_{\mathrm{mix}}(G,q)=\min\{t:\max_{\sigma\in\Omega}\|P^t(\sigma,\cdot)-U_\Omega\|_{TV}\le 1/4\}$. Claim: for every $\varepsilon>0$ there are $\Delta_0$ and $C$ such that $t_{\mathrm{mix}}(G,q)\le C n^{C}$ for every graph $G$ with $\Delta(G)\ge\Delta_0$ and every integer $q\ge(1+\varepsilon)\Delta(G)$.

import Mathlib
/-! QED-M126: Glauber dynamics for colourings mixes rapidly with (1+eps)Delta colours
To sample a random proper colouring of a graph with q colours, repeat this step: pick a random
vertex and a random colour, and recolour the vertex if no neighbour already has that colour. For
large maximum degree Delta this chain is known to reach equilibrium in polynomial time once q is a
bit above (1+1/e)Delta. Conjecturally q >= Delta+2 is enough. Weakest asymptotic form: for every
eps > 0, are (1+eps)Delta colours enough once Delta is large?
Informal statement: For a finite graph G on n vertices with maximum degree Δ and q colours, let Ω
be the set of proper q-colourings and P the Glauber (Metropolis) chain on Ω: choose v ∈ V and
c ∈ [q] uniformly and set σ(v) = c if no neighbour of v has colour c. Let
t_mix(G,q) = min{t : max_{σ∈Ω} ‖P^t(σ,·) − U_Ω‖_TV ≤ 1/4}. Claim: for every ε > 0 there are Δ₀
and C such that t_mix(G,q) ≤ C·n^C for every graph G with Δ(G) ≥ Δ₀ and every integer
q ≥ (1+ε)Δ(G).
Formalization notes:
* Graphs are `SimpleGraph (Fin n)` (every finite simple graph up to isomorphism); Δ(G) is Mathlib's
  `SimpleGraph.maxDegree`.
* The chain is run on all maps `Fin n → Fin q`; `glauberStep G σ v c` recolours `v` to `c` if no
  neighbour of `v` has colour `c` and otherwise leaves `σ` unchanged (lazy Metropolis rule; the
  choice c = σ(v) is a holding step, as in the standard chain). From a proper colouring the chain
  stays among proper colourings, so `law` started at a proper σ is supported on Ω and the total
  variation distance computed over all maps equals the one over Ω.
* `trans G q σ τ = #{(v,c) : glauberStep G σ v c = τ} / (n q)` is the transition matrix;
  `law G q σ t` is the row P^t(σ,·), defined by the recursion law_{t+1}(τ) = Σ_ρ law_t(ρ) P(ρ,τ).
* `uniformProper` is the uniform distribution on Ω (0 off Ω); `tvDist μ ν = ½ Σ |μ − ν|`.
* `MixedBy G q t` says max over proper σ of the TV distance at time t is ≤ 1/4. Since
  d(t) = max_σ ‖P^t(σ,·) − π‖_TV is non-increasing for every finite Markov chain with stationary
  distribution π (here π = U_Ω, P is symmetric), "∃ t ≤ T, MixedBy G q t" is equivalent to
  t_mix ≤ T; this avoids `Nat.find`.
* Claim: ∀ ε > 0, ∃ Δ₀ C : ℕ, ∀ n G q, Δ(G) ≥ Δ₀ → q ≥ (1+ε)Δ(G) → t_mix(G,q) ≤ C·n^C.
  Δ₀ is chosen by the prover, so the range Δ+2 > q ≥ (1+ε)Δ (where the chain may be non-ergodic)
  is excluded by taking Δ₀ ≥ 2/ε, exactly as in the informal statement. Proving `Claim` = the
  asymptotic (1+o(1))Δ rapid-mixing conjecture; `¬Claim` = some ε > 0 and graphs of arbitrarily
  large degree with super-polynomial mixing at q ≥ (1+ε)Δ.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDM126
noncomputable section
open Classical

/-- `σ` is a proper colouring of `G`. -/
def IsProper {n q : ℕ} (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) (σ : Fin n → Fin q) : Prop :=
  ∀ u v : Fin n, G.Adj u v → σ u ≠ σ v

/-- One Glauber (Metropolis) update with chosen vertex `v` and colour `c`. -/
def glauberStep {n q : ℕ} (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) (σ : Fin n → Fin q) (v : Fin n) (c : Fin q) :
    Fin n → Fin q :=
  if (∀ u : Fin n, G.Adj v u → σ u ≠ c) then Function.update σ v c else σ

/-- Transition probability `P(σ, τ)` of the Glauber chain (`(v,c)` uniform on `Fin n × Fin q`). -/
def trans {n q : ℕ} (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) (σ τ : Fin n → Fin q) : ℝ :=
  ((Finset.univ.filter (fun vc : Fin n × Fin q => glauberStep G σ vc.1 vc.2 = τ)).card : ℝ) /
    ((n : ℝ) * (q : ℝ))

/-- The distribution `P^t(σ, ·)` of the chain after `t` steps, started at `σ`. -/
def law {n q : ℕ} (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) (σ : Fin n → Fin q) : ℕ → (Fin n → Fin q) → ℝ
  | 0 => fun τ => if τ = σ then 1 else 0
  | t + 1 => fun τ => ∑ ρ : Fin n → Fin q, law G σ t ρ * trans G ρ τ

/-- Number of proper colourings `|Ω|`. -/
def numProper {n q : ℕ} (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) : ℕ :=
  (Finset.univ.filter (fun σ : Fin n → Fin q => IsProper G σ)).card

/-- The uniform distribution on proper colourings. -/
def uniformProper {n q : ℕ} (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) (τ : Fin n → Fin q) : ℝ :=
  if IsProper G τ then 1 / ((numProper (q := q) G : ℕ) : ℝ) else 0

/-- Total variation distance between two functions on a finite type. -/
def tvDist {α : Type} [Fintype α] (μ ν : α → ℝ) : ℝ :=
  (1 / 2 : ℝ) * ∑ a : α, |μ a - ν a|

/-- After `t` steps, every proper starting state is within TV distance `1/4` of uniform. -/
def MixedBy {n : ℕ} (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) (q t : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ σ : Fin n → Fin q, IsProper G σ → tvDist (law G σ t) (uniformProper (q := q) G) ≤ 1 / 4

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ ε : ℝ, 0 < ε → ∃ Δ₀ C : ℕ, ∀ (n : ℕ) (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) [DecidableRel G.Adj] (q : ℕ),
    Δ₀ ≤ G.maxDegree → (1 + ε) * (G.maxDegree : ℝ) ≤ (q : ℝ) →
      ∃ t : ℕ, t ≤ C * n ^ C ∧ MixedBy G q t

end
end OpenProblems.QEDM126

title: Are graphs with no K7 minor 7-colourable?
credit: Open question recorded in arXiv:2609.17760 and earlier (Albar-Gonçalves 2018); weaker unnamed sub-question of the t=7 case of Hadwiger's conjecture.
premise_risks: The '6-colourable' version is a named-conjecture case; the claim is deliberately the weaker 7-colour statement, which is unnamed
Key 2026 source arXiv:2609.17760 is an unrefereed preprint (its statement of openness is corroborated by the refereed 8-colourability literature)
Must make sure the OpenAI 'linear list colouring bound in terms of Hadwiger number' does not give a constant <= 7 for t=7 (its abstract-level claim is a linear bound, constant not small)
plain: A graph has a K7 minor if one can find 7 disjoint connected groups of vertices with an edge between every two groups. Graphs with no K7 minor are known to be colourable with 8 colours, and the t=7 case of Hadwiger's conjecture predicts that 6 suffice, but nobody can even show that 7 colours always suffice. Prove (or disprove) that every graph with no K7 minor can be properly coloured with 7 colours.
math: Let $G$ be a finite simple graph with no $K_7$ minor, i.e. there are no pairwise disjoint nonempty sets $B_1,\dots,B_7\subseteq V(G)$ with each $G[B_i]$ connected and at least one edge between $B_i$ and $B_j$ for all $i\ne j$. Claim: $\chi(G)\le 7$. (Known: $\chi(G)\le 8$.)

import Mathlib
/-! QED-M127: Are graphs with no K7 minor 7-colourable?
Graphs with no K7 minor are known to be 8-colourable, and the t = 7 case of Hadwiger's
conjecture predicts 6 colours, but even 7 colours is open. Prove or disprove that every graph
with no K7 minor is properly 7-colourable.
Informal statement: Let G be a finite simple graph with no K₇ minor, i.e. there are no pairwise
disjoint nonempty sets B₁,…,B₇ ⊆ V(G) with each G[Bᵢ] connected and at least one edge between
Bᵢ and Bⱼ for all i ≠ j. Claim: χ(G) ≤ 7. (Known: χ(G) ≤ 8.)
Formalization notes: Finite graphs are taken on vertex type `Fin n` (every finite simple graph
is isomorphic to one of these, and both minor-containment and colourability are isomorphism
invariant). `HasCliqueMinor G t` is the branch-set definition of a K_t minor: t sets of
vertices, each inducing a connected subgraph (`SimpleGraph.Connected` of the induced graph
`G.induce (B i)`, which includes nonemptiness), pairwise disjoint, and pairwise joined by an
edge. This is the standard equivalent of "K_t is obtained from G by deleting and contracting".
Colourability is Mathlib's `SimpleGraph.Colorable` (a proper colouring with colours in `Fin 7`).
`Claim` = every K₇-minor-free finite graph is 7-colourable; `¬Claim` = an explicit finite
K₇-minor-free graph with chromatic number 8.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDM127
noncomputable section

/-- `G` has a `K_t` minor, via branch sets. -/
def HasCliqueMinor {V : Type} (G : SimpleGraph V) (t : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ B : Fin t → Set V,
    (∀ i : Fin t, (G.induce (B i)).Connected) ∧
    (∀ i j : Fin t, i ≠ j → Disjoint (B i) (B j)) ∧
    (∀ i j : Fin t, i ≠ j → ∃ u ∈ B i, ∃ v ∈ B j, G.Adj u v)

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ (n : ℕ) (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)), ¬ HasCliqueMinor G 7 → G.Colorable 7

end
end OpenProblems.QEDM127

title: Monochromatic rectangles in low-rank Boolean matrices: beating 2^{-sqrt r}
credit: Weakening of the log-rank conjecture (Lovász–Saks 1988); rectangle formulation Nisan–Wigderson 1995; sqrt barrier from Lovett 2016 and Sudakov–Tomon 2024.
premise_risks: This is an unnamed weakening of a person-associated famous conjecture (log-rank, Lovász–Saks); permitted under the sub-question rule but scorer may judge it a famous problem in disguise
Exponent target c<1/2 is natural (first polynomial improvement) but any such result would be a major breakthrough: very hard
plain: Take any m-by-n matrix of 0s and 1s whose real rank is r. It is known that it always contains an all-0 or all-1 submatrix (some rows times some columns) covering at least a 2^{-O(sqrt r)} fraction of the entries. Can sqrt r be replaced by r^c for some c < 1/2? By a standard reduction this is the same as a communication protocol of cost O(r^c), beating the current sqrt(rank) bound on the way to the log-rank conjecture.
math: Do there exist constants $c<1/2$ and $C>0$ such that for all $m,n\ge1$ and every $M\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}$ with $r=\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb R}(M)\ge1$ there are $A\subseteq[m]$, $B\subseteq[n]$, $b\in\{0,1\}$ with $M_{ij}=b$ for all $(i,j)\in A\times B$ and $|A||B|\ge mn\,2^{-Cr^{c}}$? (By the Nisan--Wigderson/Lovett recursion this is equivalent, up to constants, to $D(M)=O(\operatorname{rank}(M)^{c})$ for all Boolean $M$.)

title: Positivity of order-6 linear recurrences: decidable?
credit: Open problem as posed by Ouaknine and Worrell (2014); restated in Ibrahim et al. arXiv:2412.08576.
premise_risks: The rational-to-integer reduction I sketched (scaling by d^n) changes the recurrence coefficients but preserves order and sign; standard but worth a one-line check by the formalizer.

plain: An integer sequence obeying a fixed linear recurrence u_{n+6} = a_1 u_{n+5} + ... + a_6 u_n is determined by six coefficients and six starting values. Is there an algorithm that, given these twelve integers, decides whether every term of the sequence is nonnegative? Such an algorithm exists for recurrences of order at most 5; order 6 is the first open case.

Let $\mathrm{Pos}=\{(a,c)\in\mathbb Z^{12}: u^{a,c}_n\ge 0\ \forall n\in\mathbb N\}$. Problem: is $\mathrm{Pos}$ a decidable (computable) subset of $\mathbb Z^{12}$? Board Claim (either direction accepted): $\mathrm{Pos}$ is decidable, or $\mathrm{Pos}$ is undecidable.

import Mathlib
/-! QED-M130: Positivity of order-6 linear recurrences: decidable?
An integer sequence obeying a fixed linear recurrence u_{n+6} = a_1 u_{n+5} + ... + a_6 u_n is determined by six coefficients and six starting values. Is there an algorithm that, given these twelve integers, decides whether every term of the sequence is nonnegative? Such an algorithm exists for recurrences of order at most 5; order 6 is the first open case.
Informal statement: For $a=(a_1,\dots,a_6)\in\mathbb Z^6$ and $c=(c_0,\dots,c_5)\in\mathbb Z^6$ let $u=u^{a,c}$ be defined by $u_n=c_n$ ($n<6$) and $u_{n+6}=\sum_{i=1}^6 a_iu_{n+6-i}$. Let $\mathrm{Pos}=\{(a,c)\in\mathbb Z^{12}: u^{a,c}_n\ge 0\ \forall n\in\mathbb N\}$. Is $\mathrm{Pos}$ a decidable (computable) subset of $\mathbb Z^{12}$? Claim (either direction accepted): $\mathrm{Pos}$ is decidable, or $\mathrm{Pos}$ is undecidable.
Formalization notes:
* `lrs a c` is the integer sequence with initial values c 0, …, c 5 and recurrence u(n+6) = a 0·u(n+5) + a 1·u(n+4) + … + a 5·u(n) (so `a i` is a_{i+1}). Defined by structural recursion.
* Computability uses Mathlib's `ComputablePred` (Partrec/Computable, i.e. Turing-computable via partial recursive functions). Inputs are encoded as a pair of lists of pairs of naturals: (p, q) codes the integer p − q, and an instance is valid only if both lists have length exactly 6 (invalid inputs are rejected, i.e. not in `PosInput`). Decoding and length checks are primitive recursive, and every integer 12-tuple has a code, so `PosInput` is computable iff Pos ⊆ ℤ¹² is computable under any standard encoding. Using ℕ-pairs avoids relying on a `Primcodable ℤ` instance.
* Degenerate instances (a_6 = 0, i.e. order < 6) are included; they are decidable by Ouaknine–Worrell, so including them changes nothing. Rational coefficients/initial values (the literature's usual setting) reduce to integers by clearing denominators (u'_n = D^n·E·u_n satisfies an integer recurrence of the same order and has the same signs), so the integer version is equivalent.
* `Claim` = Positivity for order-6 integer LRS is decidable. `¬Claim` = it is undecidable. Either settles the problem (the board accepts either direction). Pos is co-r.e. (a negative term is found by search), so `Claim` is equivalent to Pos being r.e.

namespace OpenProblems.QEDM130

/-- The order-6 linear recurrence sequence with coefficients `a` and initial values `c`. -/
def lrs (a c : Fin 6 → ℤ) : ℕ → ℤ
  | 0 => c 0
  | 1 => c 1
  | 2 => c 2
  | 3 => c 3
  | 4 => c 4
  | 5 => c 5
  | n + 6 => a 0 * lrs a c (n + 5) + a 1 * lrs a c (n + 4) + a 2 * lrs a c (n + 3) +
      a 3 * lrs a c (n + 2) + a 4 * lrs a c (n + 1) + a 5 * lrs a c n

/-- The integer coded by a pair of naturals. -/
def decInt (p : ℕ × ℕ) : ℤ := (p.1 : ℤ) - (p.2 : ℤ)

/-- The 6-vector coded by a list (missing entries read as 0; such inputs are rejected anyway). -/
def vecOf (L : List (ℕ × ℕ)) : Fin 6 → ℤ := fun i => decInt (L.getD i.val (0, 0))

/-- The coded instance is valid and its sequence is nonnegative. -/
def PosInput (x : List (ℕ × ℕ) × List (ℕ × ℕ)) : Prop :=
  x.1.length = 6 ∧ x.2.length = 6 ∧ ∀ n : ℕ, 0 ≤ lrs (vecOf x.1) (vecOf x.2) n

/-- Positivity of order-6 integer linear recurrence sequences is decidable. -/
def Claim : Prop := ComputablePred PosInput

end OpenProblems.QEDM130

title: Is the 4-sphere algorithmically recognizable?
credit: Classical question (Novikov era); current statements in Tancer arXiv:2310.07421 and Friedl–Hirsch–Kegel arXiv:2603.23630.
premise_risks: Equivalence of the bistellar-move definition with PL homeomorphism rests on Pachner's theorem (refereed, 1991); the board statement is self-contained and does not depend on it.
Must state the move definition carefully (link condition B ∉ K and fresh vertices for the 1→6 move); a sloppy move set could change the set S.
Friedl–Hirsch–Kegel 2026 is a preprint; openness is also stated in refereed sources (Tancer).
plain: A triangulated 4-dimensional shape can be given as a finite list of 5-element vertex sets. Is there an algorithm that decides whether such a list describes the piecewise-linear 4-sphere? The question is solved (yes) in dimension 3 and known to be undecidable in every dimension 5 and above; dimension 4 is the single open case.
math: A bistellar move on a finite pure 4-dimensional simplicial complex $K$ (vertices in $\mathbb N$, given by facets) replaces $A*\partial B$ by $\partial A*B$, where $A\cap B=\emptyset$, $|A\cup B|=6$, $|A|,|B|\ge1$, $A\in K$, $\mathrm{lk}_K(A)=\partial B$ and $B\notin K$ (for $|B|=1$: a fresh vertex). Let $\mathcal S$ be the set of finite complexes isomorphic to one obtained from $\partial\Delta^5$ by finitely many bistellar moves; by Pachner's theorem these are exactly the combinatorial triangulations of the PL 4-sphere. Decide whether $\mathcal S$ is a decidable set. Board claim (either direction accepted): give an algorithm deciding membership in $\mathcal S$, or prove that none exists.
lean:
import Mathlib
/-! QED-M131: Is the 4-sphere algorithmically recognizable?
A triangulated 4-dimensional shape can be given as a finite list of 5-element vertex sets. Is there
an algorithm that decides whether such a list describes the piecewise-linear 4-sphere? The question
is solved (yes) in dimension 3 and known to be undecidable in every dimension 5 and above;
dimension 4 is the single open case.
Informal statement: A bistellar move on a finite pure 4-dimensional simplicial complex K (vertices
in ℕ, given by facets) replaces A * ∂B by ∂A * B, where A ∩ B = ∅, |A ∪ B| = 6, |A|, |B| ≥ 1,
A ∈ K, lk_K(A) = ∂B and B ∉ K (for |B| = 1: a fresh vertex). Let 𝒮 be the set of finite complexes
isomorphic to one obtained from ∂Δ⁵ by finitely many bistellar moves; by Pachner's theorem these
are exactly the combinatorial triangulations of the PL 4-sphere. Decide whether 𝒮 is a decidable
set. Board claim (either direction accepted): give an algorithm deciding membership in 𝒮, or prove
that none exists.
Formalization notes:
* A complex is its set of facets `K : Finset (Finset ℕ)`; its faces are all subsets of facets
  (`IsFace`, including ∅). Complexes reachable from ∂Δ⁵ always have all facets of size 5.
* Link: `τ ∈ lk_K(A)` iff `τ ∩ A = ∅` and `τ ∪ A` is a face. `lk_K(A) = ∂B` is stated as: for
  every finset τ, (τ ∩ A = ∅ ∧ τ ∪ A face) ↔ τ ⊊ B. (For |B| = 1 this says A is a facet.)
* Move (`BistellarStep K K'`): A, B disjoint, |A|,|B| ≥ 1, |A ∪ B| = 6, A a face, link
  condition, B not a face of K. Given the link condition the facets of K containing A are exactly
  A ∪ (B∖{b}); they are removed and replaced by (A∖{a}) ∪ B for a ∈ A. The condition "B not a face"
  is the standard requirement; for |B| = 1 it says exactly that the new vertex is fresh, and it
  guarantees the new facets are not already present. This is Pachner's set of bistellar moves.
* ∂Δ⁵ = all 5-subsets of {0,…,5}. Isomorphism = relabelling vertices by a permutation of ℕ.
  `InS K` := K is isomorphic to a complex reachable from ∂Δ⁵ by finitely many moves
  (`Relation.ReflTransGen`).
* Inputs to an algorithm are codes `List (List ℕ)` (a list of vertex lists; `decodeComplex`
  turns each into a finset and the list into a finset of facets), which carry Mathlib's
  `Primcodable` structure; every finite complex has a code, and the decoded set is computable from
  the code, so decidability of `InS` on codes is the same as decidability of 𝒮.
* Claim := `ComputablePred (fun c => InS (decodeComplex c))` (Mathlib's notion of a decidable
  predicate on a `Primcodable` type, i.e. a partial-recursive total decision procedure).
  Proving `Claim` = 4-sphere recognition is decidable; `¬Claim` = it is undecidable. Both are
  accepted.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDM131
noncomputable section

/-- `σ` is a face of the complex with facet set `K`. -/
def IsFace (K : Finset (Finset ℕ)) (σ : Finset ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ F ∈ K, σ ⊆ F

/-- The bistellar move with parameters `A`, `B` turns `K` into `K'`. -/
def BistellarMove (K : Finset (Finset ℕ)) (A B : Finset ℕ) (K' : Finset (Finset ℕ)) : Prop :=
  Disjoint A B ∧ A.Nonempty ∧ B.Nonempty ∧ (A ∪ B).card = 6 ∧ IsFace K A ∧
    (∀ τ : Finset ℕ, (Disjoint τ A ∧ IsFace K (τ ∪ A)) ↔ τ ⊂ B) ∧
    ¬ IsFace K B ∧
    K' = K.filter (fun F => ¬ A ⊆ F) ∪ A.image (fun a => (A.erase a) ∪ B)

/-- One bistellar move. -/
def BistellarStep (K K' : Finset (Finset ℕ)) : Prop :=
  ∃ A B : Finset ℕ, BistellarMove K A B K'

/-- The boundary of the 5-simplex on vertices `{0,…,5}`. -/
def boundarySimplex5 : Finset (Finset ℕ) :=
  (Finset.range 6).powersetCard 5

/-- Two facet sets are isomorphic: related by a relabelling of the vertices. -/
def ComplexIso (L K : Finset (Finset ℕ)) : Prop :=
  ∃ e : Equiv.Perm ℕ, K = L.image (fun F => F.map e.toEmbedding)

/-- `K` is a combinatorial triangulation of the PL 4-sphere (Pachner): isomorphic to a complex
reachable from `∂Δ⁵` by bistellar moves. -/
def InS (K : Finset (Finset ℕ)) : Prop :=
  ∃ L : Finset (Finset ℕ), Relation.ReflTransGen BistellarStep boundarySimplex5 L ∧ ComplexIso L K

/-- Decoding an input: a list of vertex lists, read as a set of facets. -/
def decodeComplex (c : List (List ℕ)) : Finset (Finset ℕ) :=
  (c.map List.toFinset).toFinset

def Claim : Prop :=
  ComputablePred (fun c : List (List ℕ) => InS (decodeComplex c))

end
end OpenProblems.QEDM131

title: The 4/3 integrality gap of the subtour LP for metric TSP
credit: Folklore '4/3 conjecture' (Goemans 1995; Williamson 1990s); statement source: Karlin–Klein–Oveis Gharan 2022; Cook–Hougardy–Petrich 2026.
premise_risks: Very famous problem (low novelty, high importance)
Cook–Hougardy–Petrich computations are an unrefereed 2026 preprint (only used as supporting evidence)
plain: Take n cities with distances that satisfy the triangle inequality. The subtour LP relaxes 'pick a tour' to 'put fractional weights on the roads so every city has total weight 2, and every split of the cities into two groups is crossed by total weight at least 2'. Is the cheapest tour always at most 4/3 times the cheapest fractional solution? Known examples show 4/3 cannot be lowered; the best proven factor is only slightly below 3/2.
math: Let $n\ge3$ and let $c:\binom{[n]}{2}\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}$ satisfy $c_{uw}\le c_{uv}+c_{vw}$. Let $x\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{\binom{[n]}{2}}$ satisfy $x(\delta(v))=2$ for all $v\in[n]$ and $x(\delta(S))\ge2$ for all $\emptyset\ne S\subsetneq[n]$. Prove that some Hamiltonian cycle $H$ on $[n]$ has $c(H)\le\frac43\sum_e c_ex_e$. (Equivalently: the integrality ratio of the subtour/Held--Karp relaxation of metric TSP equals $4/3$; the lower bound $4/3$ is known.)

/-! QED-M132: The 4/3 integrality gap of the subtour LP for metric TSP
Take n cities with distances that satisfy the triangle inequality. The subtour LP relaxes 'pick a tour' to 'put fractional weights on the roads so every city has total weight 2, and every split of the cities into two groups is crossed by total weight at least 2'. Is the cheapest tour always at most 4/3 times the cheapest fractional solution? Known examples show 4/3 cannot be lowered; the best proven factor is only slightly below 3/2.
Informal statement: Let $n\ge3$ and let $c:\binom{[n]}{2}\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}$ satisfy $c_{uw}\le c_{uv}+c_{vw}$. Let $x\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{\binom{[n]}{2}}$ satisfy $x(\delta(v))=2$ for all $v\in[n]$ and $x(\delta(S))\ge2$ for all $\emptyset\ne S\subsetneq[n]$. Prove that some Hamiltonian cycle $H$ on $[n]$ has $c(H)\le\frac43\sum_e c_ex_e$. (Equivalently: the integrality ratio of the subtour/Held--Karp relaxation of metric TSP equals $4/3$; the lower bound $4/3$ is known.)
Formalization notes: Cities are `Fin n`. An undirected edge {i,j} (i ≠ j) is represented by
the ordered pairs (i,j) and (j,i); costs `c` and LP values `x` are functions `Fin n → Fin n → ℝ`
required to be symmetric, so `c i j = c j i` is the cost of edge {i,j} and `x i j = x j i` its
LP weight. Diagonal entries play no role in the LP (all sums below skip i = j) except that
we ask `c i i = 0` so that the triangle inequality may be stated for all triples; any metric on
the edges extends this way, so no instance is lost.
* metric: `c ≥ 0`, symmetric, `c i i = 0`, `c u w ≤ c u v + c v w` for all u v w.
* subtour LP feasibility: `x ≥ 0`, symmetric, degree constraint `∑_{j ≠ v} x v j = 2` for every v,
  cut constraint `∑_{i ∈ S} ∑_{j ∉ S} x i j ≥ 2` for every nonempty proper S (each crossing edge is
  counted once, since i ∈ S, j ∉ S fixes its orientation).
* LP objective: `∑_{i<j} c i j * x i j` (each undirected edge once).
* Hamiltonian cycle: a cyclic permutation σ of `Fin n` whose support is everything; its tour cost is
  `∑_v c v (σ v)`, each edge of the cycle counted once (n ≥ 3, so σ v ≠ v and the n edges
  {v, σ v} are distinct).
Claim says: for every n ≥ 3, every metric c and every feasible x, the optimal tour costs at most
4/3 times the LP value of x (in particular of the LP optimum). This is exactly "integrality gap ≤ 4/3".
Proving ¬Claim means exhibiting a metric instance and feasible x with every tour > (4/3)·c(x).
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDM132
noncomputable section

/-- `c` is a metric (semimetric with zero diagonal) on `Fin n`. -/
def IsMetricCost (n : ℕ) (c : Fin n → Fin n → ℝ) : Prop :=
  (∀ i j : Fin n, 0 ≤ c i j) ∧ (∀ i j : Fin n, c i j = c j i) ∧ (∀ i : Fin n, c i i = 0) ∧
    ∀ u v w : Fin n, c u w ≤ c u v + c v w

/-- `x` is a feasible point of the subtour (Held–Karp) LP on the complete graph on `Fin n`. -/
def SubtourFeasible (n : ℕ) (x : Fin n → Fin n → ℝ) : Prop :=
  (∀ i j : Fin n, 0 ≤ x i j) ∧ (∀ i j : Fin n, x i j = x j i) ∧
    (∀ v : Fin n, ∑ j ∈ (Finset.univ.filter fun j : Fin n => j ≠ v), x v j = 2) ∧
    ∀ S : Finset (Fin n), S.Nonempty → S ≠ Finset.univ →
      2 ≤ ∑ i ∈ S, ∑ j ∈ Sᶜ, x i j

/-- LP objective: each undirected edge `{i,j}` counted once, via `i < j`. -/
def lpCost (n : ℕ) (c x : Fin n → Fin n → ℝ) : ℝ :=
  ∑ i : Fin n, ∑ j ∈ (Finset.univ.filter fun j : Fin n => i < j), c i j * x i j

/-- A Hamiltonian cycle on `Fin n`: a single cycle permutation moving every vertex. -/
def IsHamCycle (n : ℕ) (σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) : Prop :=
  σ.IsCycle ∧ σ.support = Finset.univ

/-- Cost of the tour `v → σ v`. -/
def tourCost (n : ℕ) (c : Fin n → Fin n → ℝ) (σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) : ℝ :=
  ∑ v : Fin n, c v (σ v)

def Claim : Prop :=
  ∀ n : ℕ, 3 ≤ n → ∀ c : Fin n → Fin n → ℝ, IsMetricCost n c →
    ∀ x : Fin n → Fin n → ℝ, SubtourFeasible n x →
      ∃ σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n), IsHamCycle n σ ∧ tourCost n c σ ≤ (4 / 3 : ℝ) * lpCost n c x

end
end OpenProblems.QEDM132

title: Polynomial-size linear extended formulations for stable set polytopes of perfect graphs
credit: Question going back to Yannakakis (1991); restated in Aprile–Faenza (2018), Hu–Laurent (2017), Fiorini et al.
premise_risks: Sometimes cited as 'Yannakakis' question' (but not a named conjecture; the statement itself is a plain question)
Could be resolved negatively by a communication-complexity lower bound for CIS on perfect graphs; checked none known as of 2026
plain: For a perfect graph, the convex hull of its independent sets is cut out by the inequalities 'each clique contains at most one chosen vertex', and maximum-weight independent set is solvable in polynomial time, but only via semidefinite programming. Is this polytope always the projection of a polytope with polynomially many facets, i.e. does it have a polynomial-size linear program? The best upper bound is n^{O(log n)}, and lower bounds are barely superlinear.
math: For a graph $G$ on $[n]$ let $M_G$ have rows indexed by cliques $K$, columns by stable sets $S$, entries $M_G(K,S)=1-|K\cap S|\ (\ge0)$. Determine whether there is a constant $C$ such that $\operatorname{rank}_+(M_G)\le n^C$ for every perfect graph $G$ on $n\ge2$ vertices. (By Yannakakis' theorem and $\mathrm{STAB}(G)=\mathrm{QSTAB}(G)$, $\operatorname{rank}_+(M_G)$ equals the linear extension complexity of $\mathrm{STAB}(G)$ up to an additive $O(n)$.) Known: $\operatorname{rank}_+(M_G)\le n^{O(\log n)}$.

Determine whether there is a constant $C$ such that $\operatorname{rank}_+(M_G)\le n^C$ for every perfect graph $G$ on $n\ge2$ vertices. (By Yannakakis' theorem and $\mathrm{STAB}(G)=\mathrm{QSTAB}(G)$, $\operatorname{rank}_+(M_G)$ equals the linear extension complexity of $\mathrm{STAB}(G)$ up to an additive $O(n)$.) Known: $\operatorname{rank}_+(M_G)\le n^{O(\log n)}$.
Formalization notes:
* Graphs are `SimpleGraph (Fin n)`; all notions are isomorphism-invariant.
* Cliques and stable sets are `Finset (Fin n)` with the obvious pairwise conditions (written out
  by hand; the empty set and singletons count, as in the informal statement; including the
  empty clique row (all ones) or non-maximal cliques changes rank₊ by at most n+1, since a
  non-maximal clique row is a maximal clique row plus nonnegativity slacks).
* Perfect: for every vertex subset s, the induced graph on s has a proper colouring with k
  colours where k is the size of some clique inside s (colours are naturals < k on s; values
  off s are irrelevant, so s = ∅ is satisfied with the empty clique). Since every colouring needs at least as
  many colours as any clique, this says exactly χ(G[s]) = ω(G[s]) for all s, i.e. G is perfect.
* Nonnegative rank ≤ r: there are nonnegative real matrices U (cliques × r) and V (r × stable
  sets) with M_G(K,S) = Σᵢ U(K,i) V(i,S) for all cliques K and stable sets S. U and V are given
  on all finsets; only their values on cliques / stable sets matter.
* Claim: ∃ C, every perfect graph on n ≥ 2 vertices has rank₊(M_G) ≤ n^C, i.e. stable set
  polytopes of perfect graphs have polynomial linear extension complexity. ¬Claim: for every C
  some perfect graph has rank₊(M_G) > n^C (superpolynomial lower bound). The trivial
  factorisation has r = number of stable sets (exponential), so neither side is trivial.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDM133
noncomputable section

/-- `K` is a clique of `G`. -/
def IsCliqueF {n : ℕ} (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) (K : Finset (Fin n)) : Prop :=
  ∀ x ∈ K, ∀ y ∈ K, x ≠ y → G.Adj x y

/-- `S` is a stable (independent) set of `G`. -/
def IsStableF {n : ℕ} (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) (S : Finset (Fin n)) : Prop :=
  ∀ x ∈ S, ∀ y ∈ S, ¬ G.Adj x y

/-- `G` is perfect: every induced subgraph `G[s]` can be properly coloured with as many colours
as the size of some clique contained in `s` (equivalently χ(G[s]) = ω(G[s])). -/
def IsPerfect {n : ℕ} (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) : Prop :=
  ∀ s : Finset (Fin n), ∃ K : Finset (Fin n), K ⊆ s ∧ IsCliqueF G K ∧
    ∃ c : Fin n → ℕ, (∀ x ∈ s, c x < K.card) ∧
      ∀ x ∈ s, ∀ y ∈ s, G.Adj x y → c x ≠ c y

/-- The clique/stable-set slack matrix `M_G(K,S) = 1 - |K ∩ S|`. -/
def slack {n : ℕ} (K S : Finset (Fin n)) : ℝ := 1 - ((K ∩ S).card : ℝ)

/-- `rank₊(M_G) ≤ r`. -/
def NonnegRankLE {n : ℕ} (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) (r : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ U : Finset (Fin n) → Fin r → ℝ, ∃ V : Fin r → Finset (Fin n) → ℝ,
    (∀ K : Finset (Fin n), ∀ i : Fin r, 0 ≤ U K i) ∧
    (∀ i : Fin r, ∀ S : Finset (Fin n), 0 ≤ V i S) ∧
    ∀ K S : Finset (Fin n), IsCliqueF G K → IsStableF G S →
      slack K S = ∑ i : Fin r, U K i * V i S

/-- Stable set polytopes of perfect graphs have polynomial-size linear extended formulations. -/
def Claim : Prop :=
  ∃ C : ℕ, ∀ n : ℕ, 2 ≤ n → ∀ G : SimpleGraph (Fin n), IsPerfect G →
    ∃ r : ℕ, r ≤ n ^ C ∧ NonnegRankLE G r

end
end OpenProblems.QEDM133

/-- Maximum size of a binary code of length `n` with minimum Hamming distance at least `d`. -/

    ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in Filter.atTop,
      (A2 n ⌈(1 / 2 - ε) * (n : ℝ)⌉₊ : ℝ) ≤ (2 : ℝ) ^ ((K * ε ^ 2 + η) * (n : ℝ))

end
end OpenProblems.QEDM134

title: Is the Shannon capacity of a graph computable?
credit: Alon-Lubetzky (2006); Boche-Deppe (2020)

plain: The Shannon capacity Theta(G) of a finite graph is the limit of alpha(G^k)^{1/k}, where alpha is the independence number of the k-th strong power. Every alpha(G^k) is computable, so one can list ever better lower bounds, but no algorithm is known that produces upper bounds converging to Theta(G). Decide whether some algorithm, given G and a rational q, halts exactly when Theta(G) < q (equivalently, whether Theta is a computable function).
math: Encode finite simple graphs and rationals as natural numbers and let $\Theta(G)=\sup_k\alpha(G^{\boxtimes k})^{1/k}$. Determine whether $U=\{(G,q):\Theta(G)<q\}$ is recursively enumerable. (Since $\{(G,q):\Theta(G)>q\}$ is r.e., $U$ is r.e. iff $G\mapsto\Theta(G)$ is a computable real-valued function.) A weaker open subquestion: is $\Theta(G)$ a computable real for every $G$ (e.g. $G=C_7$)?

exactly when Θ(G) < q (equivalently, whether Θ is a computable function).
Informal statement: Encode finite simple graphs and rationals as natural numbers and let
$\Theta(G)=\sup_k\alpha(G^{\boxtimes k})^{1/k}$. Determine whether $U=\{(G,q):\Theta(G)<q\}$ is recursively
enumerable. (Since $\{(G,q):\Theta(G)>q\}$ is r.e., $U$ is r.e. iff $G\mapsto\Theta(G)$ is a computable
real-valued function.)
Formalization notes: A graph code is (n, l) : ℕ × List (ℕ × ℕ); it denotes the simple graph on Fin n in which
u ~ v iff u ≠ v and (u, v) or (v, u) occurs in l (pairs with an entry ≥ n are ignored). Every finite simple graph
arises (up to isomorphism; Θ is an isomorphism invariant). A rational threshold is a code (a, b) : ℕ × ℕ denoting
a/(b+1); negative thresholds are omitted since Θ ≥ 0 makes Θ < q false for them (a computable, trivial part). The
k-th strong power G^⊠k has vertex set Fin k → Fin n, with σ ~ τ iff σ ≠ τ and for every coordinate i, σ i = τ i or
σ i ~ τ i. α is the maximum size of an independent finset (a set of ℕ bounded by the number of vertices, so sSup is
the true maximum). Θ(G) = sup_{k ≥ 1} α(G^⊠k)^{1/k} (real rpow), which equals the limit by Fekete's lemma
(supermultiplicativity); the family is bounded by n so the iSup is the true supremum. "r.e." is Mathlib's `REPred`
(the predicate is the domain of a partial recursive function) on the Primcodable type of codes.
`Claim` = U is r.e. (equivalently Θ is computable). `¬Claim` = U is not r.e. (Θ is not computable). The weaker
subquestion (is Θ(C₇) a computable real?) is not encoded.
-/
namespace OpenProblems.QEDM135

noncomputable section

open Classical

/-- The graph on Fin n coded by an edge list: u ~ v iff u ≠ v and (u, v) or (v, u) occurs in the list. -/
def toGraph (c : ℕ × List (ℕ × ℕ)) : SimpleGraph (Fin c.1) :=
  SimpleGraph.fromRel fun u v : Fin c.1 => ((u : ℕ), (v : ℕ)) ∈ c.2

/-- The k-th strong power G^⊠k on Fin k → V: σ ~ τ iff σ ≠ τ and each coordinate is equal or adjacent
(the relation is already symmetric, so `fromRel` adds nothing beyond σ ≠ τ). -/
def strongPow {V : Type} (G : SimpleGraph V) (k : ℕ) : SimpleGraph (Fin k → V) :=
  SimpleGraph.fromRel fun σ τ : Fin k → V => ∀ i : Fin k, σ i = τ i ∨ G.Adj (σ i) (τ i)

/-- Independence number: the largest size of a finset with no two adjacent elements. -/
def indepNum {V : Type} (G : SimpleGraph V) : ℕ :=
  sSup {m : ℕ | ∃ s : Finset V, s.card = m ∧ ∀ a ∈ s, ∀ b ∈ s, ¬ G.Adj a b}

/-- Shannon capacity Θ(G) = sup_{k≥1} α(G^⊠k)^{1/k}. -/
def shannonCap {V : Type} (G : SimpleGraph V) : ℝ :=
  ⨆ k : ℕ, ((indepNum (strongPow G (k + 1)) : ℕ) : ℝ) ^ ((1 : ℝ) / ((k : ℝ) + 1))

/-- The nonnegative rational a/(b+1). -/
def qOf (p : ℕ × ℕ) : ℝ := (p.1 : ℝ) / ((p.2 : ℝ) + 1)

def Claim : Prop :=
  REPred (fun p : (ℕ × List (ℕ × ℕ)) × (ℕ × ℕ) => shannonCap (toGraph p.1) < qOf p.2)

end

end OpenProblems.QEDM135

title: The MDS conjecture over fields of odd characteristic
credit: MDS conjecture (Segre 1955 problem as reformulated in coding theory); progress by Ball, Ball–De Beule, X. Fan (2026).
